module_title: Tile Making: From Clay to Finished Product

lessons.title: Designing Tile Shapes and Sizes
lessons.body: Start by deciding what your tile will be used for. Floor tiles in a busy market need to be at least 30 cm x 30 cm and 10 mm thick. Wall tiles can be smaller, like 20 cm x 20 cm and 6 mm thick. Roof tiles are usually 40 cm long and 25 cm wide, with a curve or interlocking edge. Draw your design on paper first, using a ruler and pencil. Make a wooden or metal template so every tile is the same. In Africa, common shapes are squares, rectangles, and hexagons. For interlocking tiles, you need a tongue on one side and a groove on the other. Measure twice, cut once. Use a jigsaw or angle grinder to cut your template from 12 mm plywood or 3 mm steel. Sand the edges smooth so clay doesn't stick. Test your template by pressing it into soft clay. If the clay sticks, dust it with fine sand or talcum powder. Remember that clay shrinks about 10% when drying and firing. So if you want a finished tile of 30 cm, make your mold 33 cm. For mass production, you'll need multiple molds. Keep them identical by stacking templates and cutting together. Also think about drainage and grip. Floor tiles should have a slightly rough surface to prevent slipping. Roof tiles need a channel for water to run off. Draw your design with these practical points in mind. Finally, make a sample tile, dry it, and fire it. Check if the size and shape are what you wanted. Adjust your template if needed. This step saves you from wasting hundreds of tiles later.

lessons.title: Mass Production of Tiles Using Press Molds
lessons.body: To make many tiles quickly, you need a press mold. A simple hand press is a steel frame with a top and bottom plate. You fill the bottom plate with clay, then pull a lever to press the top plate down. This compacts the clay and gives a smooth surface. For a small workshop, you can make a press from a car jack and a strong steel frame. But for real mass production, use a hydraulic press that can apply 20 to 50 tons of pressure. That sounds expensive, but you can hire one or build a manual press with a 2-ton car jack. The key is consistent pressure. Too little pressure and the tile is weak; too much and it cracks. Start with 10 tons for a 30 cm x 30 cm tile. The clay must be prepared well. Mix dry clay powder with 15% water by weight. Let it sit for 24 hours to even out the moisture. Then wedge it to remove air bubbles. Air bubbles cause tiles to explode in the kiln. For each tile, weigh out the same amount of clay. A 30 cm x 30 cm tile that is 10 mm thick needs about 2.5 kg of clay. Place the clay in the mold, press down, and release. Remove the tile and place it on a drying board. You can make 100 tiles per hour with a two-person team: one fills and presses, one removes and stacks. Dry the tiles slowly in the shade for 3 to 5 days. Then fire them. With good molds and a steady rhythm, you can produce 500 tiles per day. That's enough to roof a small house or floor a shop. Remember to keep your molds clean and oiled with used engine oil so clay doesn't stick. Replace worn molds every 1000 tiles.

lessons.title: Creating Interlocking Tiles for Roofs and Floors
lessons.body: Interlocking tiles save time and mortar because they fit together like puzzle pieces. For roofs, the most common design in Africa is the S-shaped tile or the pantile. Each tile has a raised ridge on one side and a groove on the other. When you lay them, the ridge of one tile fits into the groove of the next. This stops rain from blowing in. To make them, you need a mold with a curved profile. You can carve a wooden mold from hardwood like mahogany or iroko. Or weld a steel mold. The mold should be 40 cm long, 25 cm wide, and have a 5 cm curve. For floors, interlocking tiles have tabs and slots on all four sides. They click together without adhesive. This is perfect for temporary floors or areas that get wet. To make floor interlocking tiles, your mold needs precise tabs. A 1 cm tab on two sides and a 1 cm slot on the other two sides works well. Use a CNC machine or a steady hand with a router to cut the mold. When pressing, fill the mold evenly. Press at 15 tons for floor tiles because they need to be dense. After pressing, trim the edges with a wire cutter while the clay is still soft. Dry the tiles on a flat rack so they don't warp. Fire them to 1000Â°C. After firing, test the interlock by fitting two tiles together. They should hold tight but still be easy to separate. For roofs, overlap each tile by 10 cm. For floors, lay them on a bed of sand and tap them down with a rubber mallet. Interlocking tiles are strong and quick to install. A team of two can lay 20 square meters of floor tiles in a day. That's faster than cement tiles. So invest in good molds and you'll save money on labour and glue.

lessons.title: Decorating Tiles with African Motifs
lessons.body: African motifs make your tiles unique and sell for a higher price. You can decorate before or after firing. Before firing, the clay is soft and you can press patterns into it. Use wooden stamps carved with Adinkra symbols, Ndebele geometric shapes, or Kente cloth patterns. To make a stamp, draw your design on a 5 cm x 5 cm block of hardwood. Carve away the background so the design stands out 3 mm. Press the stamp into the tile when the clay is leather-hard (not too wet, not too dry). Use a mallet to tap it evenly. For repeating patterns, mark the tile with a grid first. Another method is sgraffito: paint the tile with a coloured slip (clay mixed with water and pigment), let it dry, then scratch through the slip with a nail or knife to reveal the clay body underneath. This gives a two-tone effect. You can also use a slip trailer to draw lines and dots. After firing, you can paint with underglaze colours. Mix ceramic pigments with a glaze base. Common colours are iron oxide for red, copper oxide for green, and cobalt oxide for blue. Paint your motif with a brush. Then dip the tile in a clear glaze and fire again to 1050Â°C. The glaze makes the colours permanent and food-safe. For outdoor tiles, use a matte glaze that resists weathering. Remember that African motifs are often symmetrical. Use a ruler and compass to plan your design. Practice on paper first. Then make a set of tiles with the same motif. Sell them as a set for a kitchen backsplash or a tabletop. A set of 12 decorated tiles can sell for three times the price of plain tiles. So take time to learn one motif well, then repeat it perfectly.

lessons.title: Firing and Glazing Tiles for Durability
lessons.body: Firing turns soft clay into hard ceramic. You need a kiln. For small-scale production, build a kiln from firebricks and a metal drum. Or buy a second-hand electric kiln. The firing schedule is critical. First, bisque fire your tiles to 950Â°C. This drives off water and carbon. Heat slowly: 100Â°C per hour until 600Â°C, then 150Â°C per hour to 950Â°C. Hold at 950Â°C for 30 minutes. Then let it cool slowly overnight. Do not open the kiln hot or tiles will crack. After bisque firing, the tiles are porous and ready for glazing. Glaze is a glass coating. You can buy commercial glaze powder or make your own. A simple recipe: 40% feldspar, 30% silica, 20% whiting, 10% kaolin. Add water to make a creamy liquid. Dip each tile for 3 seconds. Wipe the bottom clean so it doesn't stick to the kiln shelf. For a glossy finish, fire to 1050Â°C. For a matte finish, fire to 1100Â°C. Hold for 20 minutes. The glaze melts and forms a waterproof surface. For roof tiles, you don't need glaze if you fire to 1100Â°C because the clay becomes vitrified. But glaze does add colour and makes cleaning easier. Test your glaze on a small tile first. If it bubbles or crawls, adjust the recipe. Keep a log of every firing: temperature, time, and results. After firing, check each tile for cracks, warping, or glaze defects. Only sell perfect tiles. A well-fired tile can last 50 years. That's why firing and glazing are the most important steps for durability.

lessons.title: Quality Control for Tiles
lessons.body: Quality control starts before the clay is dug. Test your clay for shrinkage, strength, and water absorption. Make 10 test tiles from each batch. Dry them and fire them. Measure before and after. Shrinkage should be between 8% and 12%. If it's more, add sand or grog. Water absorption should be less than 6% for floor tiles. To test, weigh a dry tile, boil it in water for 2 hours, then weigh again. The difference is the water absorbed. If it's too high, fire to a higher temperature. During production, check every tile for cracks, warping, and thickness. Use a caliper to measure thickness. Floor tiles must be 10 mm Â± 1 mm. Wall tiles 6 mm Â± 0.5 mm. Check the edges: they should be straight and square. Use a try square. For interlocking tiles, test the fit with a sample. They should not wobble. After firing, sort tiles into grades. Grade A: perfect, no defects. Grade B: minor chips or colour variation. Grade C: cracks or warping. Sell Grade A at full price. Grade B at 30% discount. Grade C as seconds or break them for mosaic. Also test strength. Drop a 1 kg weight from 1 meter onto a tile. It should not break. For roof tiles, test by standing on one tile (if you weigh under 80 kg). It should hold. Keep records of every batch. If a customer complains, you can trace the problem. Finally, train your workers to check each tile as they handle it. A simple checklist: size, thickness, edges, surface, and colour. Reject any tile that fails. Quality control saves your reputation. In Africa, word of mouth travels fast. Good tiles bring repeat customers.

quiz.q: What is the recommended thickness for a floor tile in a busy market?
quiz.explanation: Floor tiles in high-traffic areas need to be at least 10 mm thick for strength.

quiz.q: Why should you make your mold larger than the desired finished tile size?
options: A) To allow for clay shrinkage during drying and firing
B) To make the tile heavier
D) To fit the kiln better
quiz.explanation: Clay shrinks about 10% when drying and firing, so molds must be oversized.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a press mold in tile making?
options: B) To compact clay and create uniform tiles
quiz.explanation: A press mold compacts clay under pressure to produce consistent, strong tiles.

quiz.q: How much pressure is recommended for pressing a 30 cm x 30 cm floor tile?
quiz.explanation: About 10 tons is sufficient for a standard floor tile to achieve good density.

quiz.q: What happens if clay contains air bubbles?
options: C) Tiles may explode in the kiln
quiz.explanation: Air bubbles expand during firing and can cause tiles to crack or explode.

quiz.q: How long should pressed tiles dry in the shade before firing?
quiz.explanation: Slow drying for 3 to 5 days prevents warping and cracking.

quiz.q: What is a common interlocking roof tile design in Africa?
quiz.explanation: The S-shaped or pantile design is widely used for its water-shedding interlock.

quiz.q: What feature allows floor tiles to interlock without adhesive?
options: A) Tabs and slots on the sides
quiz.explanation: Tabs and slots on the edges allow tiles to click together.

quiz.q: How much should roof tiles overlap for effective waterproofing?
quiz.explanation: A 10 cm overlap ensures water does not penetrate during heavy rain.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to carve a wooden stamp for decorating tiles?
quiz.explanation: A chisel is used to carve the design into the wooden block.

quiz.q: What is sgraffito?
options: B) A method of scratching through slip to reveal clay
quiz.explanation: Sgraffito involves scratching through a coloured slip to create a design.

quiz.q: Which oxide is commonly used to produce a blue colour on tiles?
quiz.explanation: Cobalt oxide is a strong blue colourant in ceramics.

quiz.q: What is the typical bisque firing temperature for tiles?
quiz.explanation: Bisque firing is usually done at around 950Â°C to prepare the clay for glazing.

quiz.q: Why should you heat the kiln slowly during bisque firing?
options: B) To prevent tiles from cracking
C) To make glaze melt faster
quiz.explanation: Slow heating allows water and carbon to escape without causing cracks.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of glazing a tile?
options: B) To make it waterproof and decorative
quiz.explanation: Glaze forms a glass-like coating that makes tiles waterproof and adds colour.

quiz.q: What should you do before glazing a bisque-fired tile?
quiz.explanation: Wiping the bottom prevents glaze from sticking to the kiln shelf.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for water absorption of a fired tile?
options: B) Boil it in water and weigh before and after
C) Scratch it with a knife
D) Hit it with a hammer
quiz.explanation: Boiling and weighing shows how much water the tile absorbs, indicating porosity.

quiz.q: What is the maximum acceptable shrinkage for a clay body?
quiz.explanation: Shrinkage up to 12% is acceptable; higher causes size problems.

quiz.q: How can you test the strength of a floor tile?
options: A) Drop a 1 kg weight from 1 meter
D) Heat it in a kiln
quiz.explanation: A drop test simulates impact and checks the tile's resistance to breaking.

quiz.q: What grade should be given to a tile with a minor chip?
quiz.explanation: Grade B tiles have minor defects and are sold at a discount.

quiz.q: Why is quality control important for a tile business?
options: C) To build reputation and repeat customers
quiz.explanation: Consistent quality leads to customer trust and word-of-mouth referrals.

quiz.q: What is the recommended water content when mixing clay for pressing?
quiz.explanation: About 15% water by weight gives clay the right plasticity for pressing.

quiz.q: How many tiles can a two-person team produce per hour with a hand press?
quiz.explanation: With a good rhythm, a two-person team can make about 100 tiles per hour.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding grog to clay?
options: B) To reduce shrinkage and prevent cracking
C) To make clay melt faster
quiz.explanation: Grog is pre-fired clay that reduces shrinkage and adds strength.

quiz.q: Which African motif is commonly used for tile decoration?
quiz.explanation: Adinkra symbols from Ghana are widely used in African ceramic decoration.

quiz.q: What is the ideal firing temperature for a glossy glaze on tiles?
quiz.explanation: Glossy glazes typically mature at around 1050Â°C.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a firing log?
options: A) To track temperature, time, and results for consistency
quiz.explanation: A log helps you repeat successful firings and troubleshoot problems.

quiz.q: What is the first step in quality control for clay?
options: A) Test shrinkage and water absorption
quiz.explanation: Testing clay properties before production prevents waste.

quiz.q: How can you check if interlocking tiles fit properly?
options: B) Fit two tiles together and check for wobble
quiz.explanation: A fit test ensures the interlock is tight but easy to assemble.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of using a release agent like used engine oil on molds?
options: B) It prevents clay from sticking to the mold
quiz.explanation: Oil acts as a lubricant so pressed tiles release cleanly from the mold.
